title: The King Who Stayed Home
sum: While Joab and the army besiege Rabbah, David stays in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees Bathsheba bathing, learns she is the wife of Uriah, one of his own elite soldiers, and sends for her. She becomes pregnant. David calls Uriah home from the front to cover the pregnancy, but Uriah, loyal to the army in the field, will not go home to his wife, even when the king makes him drunk.

So David writes Joab a letter, carried by Uriah himself, ordering that Uriah be left exposed in battle. Joab obeys, and Uriah dies with other soldiers. David answers the news with a soldier's shrug and, after the mourning period, marries Bathsheba. Only in the last line does the narrator speak: what David had done looked evil in the LORD's eyes. Nothing in David's life is the same afterward.
readings: Read as the turning point of David's story

Up to this chapter, David rises: the LORD is with him, his enemies fall, and God promises him a lasting house (chapter 7). From this chapter on, his house begins to fall apart: rape, murder, rebellion and civil war. Many readers, ancient and modern, divide David's life into "before Bathsheba" and "after." The narrator draws the line in 11:27.
Read as a study in power

The verb "send" runs through the chapter. David sends Joab, sends for Bathsheba, sends for Uriah, sends a letter, and sends for Bathsheba again. Those without power wait to be sent. The chapter is a close picture of how a ruler can use people, and how a whole chain of servants, messengers and a general become part of a crime by doing as they are told.

views.H: The siege of Rabbah belongs to the Ammonite war of chapters 10–12, about 990 BC on traditional dating. Uriah and Eliam appear in the list of David's Thirty (23:34, 39), which suggests that the court story drew on real names. The detail of the letter and the battle near the wall fits what we know of siege warfare in the period.
views.C: Since Leonhard Rost (1926), most critical scholars have read chapters 9–20 and 1 Kings 1–2 as a "Succession Narrative" written near the events, perhaps under Solomon. Some date it later and read it as critical of the monarchy. Many think 11:27b and Nathan's speech in 12:7–12 were shaped by later editors who stressed God's judgment.
views.L: Literary readers admire the chapter's restraint. The narrator reports actions and almost never feelings, leaving gaps: what Bathsheba wanted, whether Uriah knew, what Joab thought. Meir Sternberg made the chapter a classic example of how biblical narrative invites the reader to fill gaps and then tests the reader's judgment.
views.J: The Talmud records a defense of David: "Whoever says David sinned is mistaken" (Shabbat 56a), arguing that soldiers gave their wives conditional divorces before battle and that Uriah was a rebel. Other sages reject the defense, and David's own confession (12:13) and Psalm 51 are held up as the model of repentance. Sanhedrin 107a says David asked God to test him as he had tested Abraham, and failed the test.
views.X: Matthew's genealogy names "the wife of Uriah" among Jesus' ancestors (Matthew 1:6), keeping the scandal in view. Christian preachers have used the chapter as a warning about how one sin leads to the next, and as a picture of the need for a better king than David.

deep.b:
The chapter tells us almost nothing about what Bathsheba thought, and readers have filled the silence in several ways, each with serious defenders.

A complicit partner. A few modern readers, notably George Nicol, suggest that Bathsheba bathed where she could be seen and accepted the king's invitation willingly. Randall Bailey argues that the marriage was a political alliance between David and a powerful family: Bathsheba's father Eliam and grandfather Ahithophel (23:34) were close to the throne, and in 1 Kings 1 she proves skillful at court. On this reading she is an agent, not only a victim.

A victim of a king's power. Others stress the grammar: David "sent," "took" and "lay"; she "came" when the king's messengers fetched her. In the ancient world no one refused a king. Nathan's parable puts all the guilt on the rich man; the lamb does nothing (12:1–4). Richard Davidson, Cheryl Exum and many others call this a rape by abuse of power, whether or not physical force was used. They argue that the bath was a religious act of purification (11:4), not a display.

A defense of David. Some rabbinic readers took a different line again. The Talmud reports the view that every soldier of David gave his wife a conditional bill of divorce before battle, so that Bathsheba was technically unmarried (Shabbat 56a), and it says she had been destined for David since the six days of creation, though he took her before the time (Sanhedrin 107a). The sages who held this did not excuse the murder of Uriah, and David's confession was still read as real guilt.

A silent character. Literary critics such as Meir Sternberg and Gale Yee point out that the narrator withholds her inner life on purpose. She is named once, then called "the woman" and "Uriah's wife." She speaks two words (11:5). The silence keeps the reader's attention on David, and lets the story ask what power does to people who have no voice. Bathsheba gets her voice later, as a queen mother who secures the throne for her son (1 Kings 1:15–31; 2:13–21).

All of these readings agree that the text holds David responsible: it is David whom Nathan accuses, and David who confesses.

deep.h: Weighing the Greek in these chapters
deep.b:
From 11:2 to 1 Kings 2:11, the main manuscript of the Greek Bible, Codex Vaticanus (which the standard Rahlfs edition mostly prints), does not carry the original Greek translation. Dominique Barthélemy showed in 1963 that this stretch was revised by Jewish scholars around the time of Jesus to match the Hebrew more closely. Scholars call the revision kaige, after its habit of rendering Hebrew gam, "also," with Greek kai ge.

This matters for weighing variants. In these chapters Vaticanus often agrees with the Leningrad Codex because it was corrected toward a Hebrew text like it, so its agreement adds little. The Lucianic or Antiochene text, preserved in a few later manuscripts, often keeps the Old Greek and so a Hebrew text older than the Leningrad Codex. And where Vaticanus still has a longer text than the Hebrew, that plus survived a revision aimed at removing such differences, which makes it more likely to be old. The Qumran scrolls of Samuel often agree with the Lucianic text against the Leningrad Codex.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two houses
deep.b: This is my own reading. The Hebrew word bayit, "house," appears again and again in chapter 11: the king's house (11:2, 8, 9), Uriah's house (11:9, 10, 11, 13), and finally David gathering Bathsheba "into his house" (11:27). In chapter 7, God promised to build David a "house," a dynasty, while David wanted to build God a house. I suggest the narrator is playing on that promise: the man who was promised a house by God destroys another man's house to fill his own. Nathan's sentence then turns the word back: "the sword will not go away from your house" (12:10). Commentators have noted the repeated "house" in chapter 11 and the link to chapter 7; reading the whole chapter as a counter-story to the dynasty promise is my own emphasis.

echoes: Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 20:1–18; Exodus 20:13–17; Leviticus 15:19–28; Leviticus 20:10; Judges 9:50–57; 1 Kings 15:5; Psalm 51:0; Matthew 1:6

settings.by: Uriah the Hittite, one of David's warriors
settings.to: King David, in Jerusalem
settings.when: when David urges him to go home to his wife, hoping to hide that Bathsheba is pregnant by David
settings.why: Uriah says the ark, the army and his commander are camping in the field, so he will not go home to eat, drink and sleep with his wife. A foreign soldier keeps the rule of holy war (compare 1 Samuel 21:5) while Israel's king has broken God's law. His loyalty is what gets him killed. Readers feel the full weight of David's guilt through Uriah's goodness.

settings.to: Joab, at the siege of Rabbah, carried by Uriah himself
settings.when: the morning after Uriah refuses for the second time to go home
settings.why: The letter orders Joab to put Uriah where the fighting is worst and then pull back so he dies. It is the first letter written in the Bible, and it is an order for murder. The king who should protect his people uses his power to kill one of them. The narrator holds back comment until the chapter's last line (11:27). Until then the reader must judge, as Nathan will in chapter 12.

settings.to: Joab, through the messenger from the battle
settings.when: after the messenger reports that Uriah is dead
settings.why: David tells Joab not to let the matter look evil in his eyes, because the sword eats one man now and another then. The words hide murder behind talk of the fortunes of war. The chapter ends by answering him: what David had done "looked evil in the LORD's eyes" (11:27). The Hebrew uses the same phrase, so David's own words are turned against him.

title: You Are the Man
sum: The LORD sends Nathan the prophet to David with a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb to feed a guest. David, furious, declares that the man deserves death. Nathan answers, "You are the man!" Speaking for God, he lists all that God gave David, names his crimes against Uriah, and announces the consequences: the sword will never leave David's house, and his wives will be taken publicly by someone close to him.

David confesses at once: "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan tells him that God has put away his sin and he will not die, but the child will. David fasts and pleads for seven days; when the child dies, he rises, worships and eats, to the confusion of his servants. Bathsheba bears a second son, Solomon, whom the LORD loves; through Nathan he is named Jedidiah. The chapter ends back at the siege, as David takes Rabbah and its king's crown.
readings: Read as a model of repentance

For Jews and Christians alike, this chapter is the Bible's great picture of confession. David does not argue or shift blame. He says two words, and the tradition of Psalm 51 fills them out. Yet forgiveness does not erase consequences: the child dies and the sword remains. The chapter holds mercy and judgment together without resolving the tension.
Read as prophet against king

Nathan is a court prophet, yet he confronts the king with a law the king is under. In much of the ancient world, a king could take whatever he wanted; here a prophet tells him he is a thief and a murderer. Many historians see this as one of the roots of the idea that rulers answer to a higher law.

views.H: Nathan was a historical court prophet who later backed Solomon (1 Kings 1). The capture of Rabbah ended the Ammonite war, and the putting of the Ammonites to forced labor matches what we know of how kings treated conquered peoples.
views.C: Many critical scholars think Nathan's oracle (12:7–12) was expanded by a later editor, since it predicts events in detail (16:22). Some think the parable and the confession are older than the oracle. The final scene at Rabbah (12:26–31) continues the war story of 10:1–11:1 and may once have followed it directly.
views.L: The parable is a perfect trap: David judges the story before he sees himself in it. The chapter mirrors chapter 11: David "sent" there, the LORD "sends" here; David "took" there, the LORD will "take" his wives here. Literary readers note how the narrator gives David a sudden calm after the child's death that his servants cannot understand.
views.J: The rabbis count four of David's children lost as the fourfold repayment of 12:6 (Yoma 22b). The Talmud says David's sin was recorded to show that repentance is open to all (Avodah Zarah 4b–5a). A verse of Psalm 51 (51:15) opens the Amidah, the central daily prayer, and the psalm is recited in penitential devotions, and Nathan's "You are the man" is a classic example of rebuke given in love.
views.X: Many churches read Psalm 51 on Ash Wednesday and in Lent, taking its heading as David's prayer from this chapter. Many Christian teachers use 12:23 to comfort parents who lose infants. The pattern of conviction, confession and forgiveness is read as a picture of the gospel (1 John 1:9), and Nathan's courage as a model for speaking truth to power.

deep.b:
Nathan says the LORD has put away David's sin and David will not die (12:13), yet in the next breath he says the child will die (12:14). Readers have struggled with this for centuries.

Some answers focus on public consequences: the sin was forgiven between David and God, but David's open contempt for the LORD's word (12:9, 14), still needed a visible answer. Others focus on the child: the child is not punished but taken, and David himself expects to go to him (12:23). Others focus on the family: ancient Israel thought of a household as one unit, and judgment on the head fell on the house. Critical scholars often add that the story explains why Solomon, not Bathsheba's first son, became the heir.

None of these answers removes the pain of the verse, and the Bible elsewhere insists that children are not punished for their parents' sins (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20). The chapter itself does not explain; it shows David pleading, then accepting.

deep.h: A sceptical reading of David's repentance
deep.b:
Not every reader takes David's confession at face value. David says "I have sinned against the LORD" (12:13), but he says nothing to Bathsheba and nothing about Uriah, and he makes no amends to anyone. When the child dies, he washes, eats and comforts Bathsheba by giving her another son (12:20–24), and within a few verses he is back at Rabbah taking a crown (12:30). David Gunn and other literary readers have suggested that the speed of his recovery shows a man who reads events in terms of what they mean for him. On this reading the confession is real but narrow, and the chapters that follow, where David fails to judge Amnon or Absalom, show a king whose repentance did not reach his household.

Others answer that confession "against the LORD" is the Bible's language for all serious wrong, including wrong to people (Genesis 39:9; Psalm 51:4), and that David's acceptance of the child's death is faith, not self-interest (12:22–23). The text itself gives the words and the actions and leaves the judgment to the reader.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the lamb and the daughter
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. In Nathan's parable the lamb is "like a daughter" (kevat, 12:3), a word that sounds like Bath-sheba's name. In the next chapter a real daughter of David, Tamar, is the victim of a king's son who takes what is not his. I suggest that the parable's lamb points two ways: back to Bathsheba and forward to Tamar. David passes judgment on the rich man without pity (12:5–6), but when his own son does the same thing to his own daughter, he is angry and does nothing (13:21). Commentators have connected the parable with Bathsheba and noted how chapter 13 mirrors chapter 11; linking the lamb "like a daughter" to Tamar is my own reading.

echoes: Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 24:16; 1 Kings 20:35–43; Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 51:0–19; Psalm 32:1–5; Luke 19:8; Matthew 1:6; Romans 4:6–8

settings.what: Nathan's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb
settings.by: Nathan the prophet, sent by the LORD
settings.to: King David, who thinks he is hearing a real case for the king's court
settings.when: after David has taken Bathsheba, had Uriah killed and married her, and the child has been born
settings.why: The parable is a trap. Nathan tells it as if it were a lawsuit about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. He wants David, as judge, to condemn the rich man before he sees himself in the story. It works: David swears the man deserves death and must repay four times (Exodus 22:1); the Greek reads "seven." Then Nathan says, "You are the man!" A king who cannot be accused openly is brought to judge himself. The lamb that "lay in his lap" and was "like a daughter" points to Bathsheba, whose name begins with the Hebrew word for "daughter." Knowing that David was meant to hear it as a court case is the key to the story.
views: Uriel Simon called this a "juridical parable": a made-up legal case told to someone who has broken the law, so that he passes judgment on himself without knowing it. The wise woman of Tekoa (14:4–17) and the prophet in 1 Kings 20:35–43 use the same method, and Simon also counted the Song of the Vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7).

Readers note that the parable does not match every detail: the rich man steals but does not kill, and the guest has no part in the real story. Many think the gaps are on purpose, so David will not see through it too soon.

settings.what: "You are the man": the LORD's judgment on David
settings.by: Nathan, speaking for the LORD, the God of Israel
settings.to: King David
settings.when: right after David condemns the rich man
settings.why: God reminds David of all he gave him and asks why he despised God's word by killing Uriah and taking his wife. The sentence fits the crime: the sword will never leave David's house, and someone close to him will take his wives in public, since David acted in secret. The rest of 2 Samuel shows it coming true through Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. Readers learn that no king stands above God's law.

settings.to: Nathan, and through him the LORD
settings.when: at the end of the oracle
settings.why: David says only, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan answers that the LORD has put away his sin and he will not die, but the child will. Unlike Saul (1 Samuel 15:24–25), David makes no excuses. Jewish and Christian readers have held this up as the model of repentance, and the heading of Psalm 51 sets that psalm at this moment.

settings.to: his servants, at the palace
settings.when: after the child dies and David gets up, washes and eats
settings.why: David says he fasted while the child lived because God might show mercy, but now nothing can bring him back: "I am the one who will go to him." The words show a king who accepts God's judgment without bitterness. Many grieving readers have found comfort in them.

settings.by: the LORD, through Nathan the prophet
settings.to: David and Bathsheba
settings.when: after the first child dies and Bathsheba bears Solomon
settings.why: The narrator says the LORD loved the boy, and Nathan brings the name Jedidiah, which means "loved by the LORD." The same prophet who announced judgment now brings a word of favor. Readers learn that God's mercy reaches past David's sin, and that Solomon, Bathsheba's son, is God's chosen heir (1 Kings 1:13).

settings.to: King David, in Jerusalem
settings.when: after Joab has taken the city's water supply
settings.why: Joab tells David to come and take the city himself, or it will be named after Joab. The message brings the story back to where it started in 11:1: David finally goes to the war he stayed home from.

traditions.q: David was forgiven, yet his child died. Does a penalty remain after forgiveness?
views: God forgives the guilt of sin and its eternal punishment, but a temporal punishment may remain, worked out through penance or purified after death (Catechism 1472–1473). The Council of Trent rejected the view that God always removes all punishment with the guilt (Session 14, canon 12), and Catholic teachers point to David.

Christ's suffering alone pays for sin, so the forgiven owe no further payment. The troubles God sends believers, like David's, are a father's discipline, not a price (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 12).
God's punishments on his children are corrections, not vengeance, and Calvin used David as his example (Institutes 3.4.31–35). Both the guilt and the penalty are fully paid by Christ.

Sin is seen more as a sickness than a legal debt. Penances given by a confessor are medicine for healing, not payments, and the effects of sin can remain as part of that healing (Kallistos Ware, The Orthodox Church).

traditions.q: David expected to go to his child. What happens to infants who die?
views: The Church entrusts unbaptized infants to God's mercy and has good grounds to hope they are saved (Catechism 1261). Limbo was a common opinion of theologians but never a defined teaching (International Theological Commission, 2007).

Infants carry no personal guilt, since the Orthodox do not teach that Adam's guilt is passed on. Gregory of Nyssa taught that infants who die are not punished and grow into the life of God (On Infants' Early Deaths).

Baptism is God's ordinary way of saving infants, so children should not be kept from it. For those who die before baptism, Luther told grieving parents to trust that God hears the prayers of believing parents (Comfort for Women Who Have Had a Miscarriage).

Elect infants who die in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit (Westminster Confession 10.3), and believing parents need not doubt the salvation of their children who die young (Canons of Dort 1.17).
Most Baptists teach that infants who die go to be with God, since they are not yet able to make moral choices (Baptist Faith and Message, article 3). This verse is often read at funerals for infants.

title: Tamar's Robe
sum: Amnon, David's firstborn, is obsessed with his half-sister Tamar. On his cousin Jonadab's advice he pretends to be sick and asks the king to send Tamar to cook for him. When they are alone he seizes her. Tamar pleads with him: such a thing is not done in Israel; it would shame her and make him a fool; he could even ask the king for her. He overpowers and rapes her, then hates her and has her thrown out. Tamar tears her royal robe, puts ashes on her head and goes away crying aloud. She lives on, desolate, in Absalom's house.

David is furious but does nothing. Absalom says nothing for two years, then invites the king's sons to his sheep-shearing feast and has Amnon killed. A false report says all the princes are dead; Jonadab knows better. Absalom flees to his grandfather in Geshur, and stays three years, while David mourns.
readings: Read as the sword in David's house

Chapter 13 repeats chapter 11 inside David's family: a king's son sees a beautiful woman, uses a trick, a servant and the king's own authority, takes her, and a killing follows. Nathan's word that the sword would not leave David's house (12:10) begins to come true.
Read as Tamar's story

Modern readers, especially since Phyllis Trible's Texts of Terror (1984), have read the chapter from Tamar's side. She is the only character who speaks wisely and morally. She names the crime, offers a lawful way out, and protests in public. Every man in the story fails her: Amnon, Jonadab, David, and in some readings Absalom, who silences her and uses her wrong for his own ends.

views.H: Marriage between half-siblings was forbidden by the laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, yet Tamar suggests the king might allow it (13:13), which may show that those laws were not enforced at David's court. Geshur was a real Aramean kingdom in the Golan, and the political marriage to Maacah fits David's diplomacy.
views.C: Critical scholars read the chapter as a key link in the Succession Narrative: it removes the firstborn Amnon and makes Absalom the heir. Some think it was written to explain how Solomon, a younger son, came to the throne. The Hebrew of 13:16, 13:21, 13:27, 13:34 and 13:39 is damaged in places, and the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek help restore it.
views.L: Literary readers note the careful echoes of Genesis 34 (Dinah, a brother's revenge), Genesis 37–38 (a robe, Judah's Tamar) and Judges 19–20 (a "disgraceful thing"). The words "love" and "hate" frame the chapter (13:1, 15, 22). Tamar's long, clear speech contrasts with Bathsheba's two words in chapter 11.
views.J: The Mishnah names Amnon's love for Tamar as the example of love "that depends on a thing" and so does not last (Avot 5:16). The Talmud says Tamar was the daughter of a captive woman who conceived her before converting, so she was not legally Amnon's sister (Sanhedrin 21a). It also reports that after this event the sages decreed against a man being alone with an unmarried woman (Sanhedrin 21a–b).
views.X: Christian readers have seen the chapter as a warning against lust, and Amnon's love-turned-hate as a picture of sin's deceit (James 1:14–15). More recently, Christian and Jewish readers alike have used Tamar's story to name sexual violence in families and communities, and to listen to victims instead of silencing them.

deep.h: Rabbinic and modern readings of Tamar
deep.b:
Rabbinic readings took the story seriously as a moral lesson. The Mishnah's teaching that love based on desire ends when the desire ends (Avot 5:16) is drawn from 13:15. The Talmud's discussion in Sanhedrin 21a explains why Tamar could say the king "will not hold me back from you": she was born to a captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:10–14) before her mother joined Israel, and so was not legally Amnon's sister. The same passage reports that this event led the sages to forbid a man and an unmarried woman to be alone together. Rabbinic readers also used Tamar's public protest, ashes and torn robe, as evidence that she did not consent, and blamed Jonadab's wicked "wisdom."

Modern readings begin with Phyllis Trible's Texts of Terror (1984), which reads the chapter as "the royal rape of wisdom": Tamar speaks like a wisdom teacher, and men of power ignore her. Feminist scholars note how the story moves from Tamar's voice to her silence: she speaks at length in 13:12–13 and 13:16, then is told by Absalom to "say nothing" (13:20) and is never heard again. Others defend Absalom as a protective brother. Pastoral readers, Jewish and Christian, have found in Tamar a voice for survivors: she names what happened as a "disgraceful thing," protests publicly, and is not to blame. Some modern scholars also note the costs of revenge: Absalom's justice is murder, and it leads to civil war.

Genesis 34, Judges 19–20 and 2 Samuel 13 share the word nevalah, "disgraceful thing," and a pattern. In Genesis, Shechem "took her and lay with her and dishonored her" (Genesis 34:2), and Jacob's sons were furious "because Shechem had done a disgraceful thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7); her brothers Simeon and Levi take revenge by massacre. In Judges, the old man begs, "do not do this disgraceful thing" (Judges 19:23), but the concubine is abused all night, and her death leads to a war that nearly destroys Benjamin. Here, Tamar uses the same words (13:12), and Absalom's revenge leads to exile and rebellion. In each story the woman's voice is barely heard after the crime, a father or husband fails her, and male revenge multiplies the violence. The stories are told without softening, as warnings.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two Tamars and a robe
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Judah's daughter-in-law Tamar (Genesis 38) and David's daughter Tamar are both women of Judah's royal line wronged by a man of their own family. The first Tamar takes off her widow's clothes and puts on a veil to claim justice (Genesis 38:14); the second tears her royal robe to protest injustice (13:19). The first is vindicated: "She is more in the right than I am" (Genesis 38:26), and her son founds David's line. The second is left desolate. I suggest the narrator, writing about David's house, expects readers to remember the founding Tamar, and that the contrast measures how far David's house has fallen from its own beginnings. The link between the robes of Tamar and Joseph is often noted; the contrast with Judah's Tamar as a deliberate frame is my own reading.

echoes: Genesis 34:1–31; Genesis 37:3; Genesis 38:1–30; Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 20:17; Deuteronomy 22:28–29; Deuteronomy 27:22; Judges 19:22–30; Judges 20:6; 1 Samuel 25:36

settings.by: Jonadab, David's nephew, called "an extremely wise man"
settings.to: Amnon, David's firstborn
settings.when: when Amnon is sick with desire for his half-sister Tamar
settings.why: Jonadab tells Amnon to pretend to be sick and ask the king to send Tamar to feed him. It is wisdom used for evil. The plan makes the king himself send his daughter into danger. Two years later the same Jonadab knows at once that Absalom has killed only Amnon (13:32–33).

settings.to: her half-brother Amnon, in his inner room
settings.when: when he seizes her, and then when he throws her out
settings.why: Tamar begs him not to do "this disgraceful thing," which "is not done in Israel," and asks him to speak to the king instead. After the rape, she says sending her away is a greater wrong. Her words name the crime in the language of Israel's law (compare Deuteronomy 22:28–29 and Genesis 34:7). No one in the story listens to her: not Amnon, not her brother Absalom, who tells her to keep quiet, and not her father, who is angry but does nothing. The narrator lets readers hear her.

settings.to: his servants, at the sheep-shearing feast at Baal-hazor
settings.when: two years after Tamar's rape
settings.why: Absalom orders his servants to strike Amnon when he is drunk, and tells them not to fear because he gives the order. The order fulfills Nathan's word that the sword would not leave David's house, and it echoes David's own order to have Uriah killed.

title: The Woman from Tekoa
sum: Joab sees that the king's heart is on Absalom and stages a scene. He brings a wise woman from Tekoa, dresses her as a widow, and gives her a story: one of her two sons killed the other, and the clan demands his death, which would wipe out her husband's name. Step by step the king promises to protect the son, finally swearing by the LORD. Then she turns the case on him: why does the king not bring home his own banished son? We are all like water spilled on the ground, she says, but God works out ways to bring the banished home.

David sees Joab's hand behind it, but agrees. Absalom returns to Jerusalem, but the king refuses to see him. The narrator describes Absalom's flawless good looks and his heavy hair. After two years, Absalom burns Joab's barley field to force a meeting, and at last the king receives him and kisses him.
readings: Read as wisdom serving politics

Joab and the wise woman use a juridical parable, like Nathan's, but for the opposite purpose: Nathan used a story to expose the king's sin, the woman uses one to win a pardon. The chapter asks whether mercy without justice is real mercy. David brings Absalom home without dealing with the murder, and the half-measure leads directly to rebellion.
Read as a theology of return

The woman's words in 14:14, that God "works out plans so the banished one is not cast away from him," have been read by Jews and Christians as one of the Old Testament's great statements of God's mercy toward exiles and sinners. The king is asked to imitate God.

views.H: The custom of blood vengeance by the next of kin, and the king's power to override it, fit what is known of early Israelite law. Tekoa was a real village south of Bethlehem. The weighing of hair "by the royal standard" suggests that a royal system of weights existed.
views.C: Critical scholars see the chapter as part of the Succession Narrative's careful build-up to Absalom's revolt. The note about Absalom's beauty and hair (14:25–27) may be an insertion preparing for 18:9, and 14:27 sits awkwardly with 18:18. Claudia Camp suggests that "wise women" held a recognized role as counselors in early Israel.
views.L: The chapter is a play within a play: Joab writes the script, the woman performs it, and the king is the audience who does not know he is in it, until he guesses. The phrases "the king's face" and "see the face" frame the second half, and the closing kiss is left without words.
views.J: Rabbinic readers praised the woman's wisdom and drew from 14:14 the teaching that God does not reject the sinner who returns. The Mishnah's lesson about Absalom's hair (Sotah 1:8) begins here: he took pride in it, and it led to his downfall.
views.X: Christians have read 14:14 as a foreshadowing of the gospel: God devising a way to bring home those banished by sin (2 Corinthians 5:18–19). Some contrast David's grudging welcome with the father's running embrace in the parable of the lost son (Luke 15:20).

deep.title: Claude's theory: a mirror of Cain and Abel
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The woman's invented story, two brothers fighting "out in the field" with no one to separate them, one killing the other, and the killer's life in danger (14:6–7), closely recalls Cain and Abel, who were "out in the country" when Cain killed his brother (Genesis 4:8), and Cain's fear that "anyone who finds me will kill me" (Genesis 4:14). In Genesis God protects the killer with a sign; in the woman's story the king protects him with an oath. I suggest Joab's script deliberately borrowed Israel's oldest story of brother-murder, so that the king would hear God's own mercy to Cain as a precedent for mercy to Absalom. Scholars have noted the general echo; reading it as Joab's deliberate strategy is my own theory.

echoes: Genesis 4:8–15; Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; Deuteronomy 25:5–10; 12:1–7; 20:16–22; 1 Kings 15:2; Luke 15:11–32; 2 Corinthians 5:18–19

settings.by: a wise woman from Tekoa, speaking words Joab put in her mouth
settings.to: King David, sitting as judge
settings.when: three years after Absalom fled for killing Amnon, when David longs for him but will not bring him back
settings.why: Like Nathan, she tells a made-up case. She says she is a widow whose son killed his brother, and the clan wants to execute him, which would leave her husband with no heir. David swears, "By the life of the LORD, not a single hair from your son's head will drop to the ground." That oath is the hook. Nathan trapped David with a verdict; she traps him with an oath. Then she turns it on him: why does he not bring his own banished son home? She adds that "we will surely die," like water poured on the ground, and that God works out ways so the banished are not cast away. When the king asks whether Joab is behind it, she admits it (14:19–20). Joab's aim is to get Absalom back. Readers see the same trap Nathan used, now used by a courtier for politics, and it leads to disaster.
views: Claudia Camp and others see her as one of a class of wise women, like the woman of Abel (20:16–22), whose speech carried public authority.
Uriel Simon groups it with Nathan's parable as a legal case told to make the king judge himself. Unlike Nathan's, it leads the king toward a choice that will cost him dearly.

title: Up the Mount of Olives
sum: Absalom builds a following. He rides in a chariot with fifty runners, stands at the city gate, tells every man with a lawsuit that his case is good but the king will not hear him, and kisses those who bow to him. So he steals the hearts of Israel. After four years he asks to go to Hebron to pay a vow, and there he has himself proclaimed king, with David's counselor Ahithophel on his side.

David flees Jerusalem with his household and his foreign guard. Ittai the Gittite refuses to leave him. David sends the ark back to Jerusalem with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, leaving the outcome to God. Then he climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, prays that Ahithophel's advice will be turned to folly, and at the top meets Hushai, whom he sends back as a spy.
readings: Read as political history

Absalom's revolt is a case study in how a popular prince can take a kingdom: royal display, grievances against the government, personal charm, a base in the old capital, a secret network across the tribes and a famous adviser. David's response is equally shrewd: he leaves the city, keeps his professional troops, and plants friends inside Absalom's court.
Read as David's humbling

The proud king of chapter 11 now walks barefoot with his head covered. He refuses to use the ark to force God's hand and says, "Let him do with me whatever looks good to him" (15:26). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see here a man who has learned from Nathan's rebuke. The heading of Psalm 3 places that psalm in this flight.

views.H: The revolt probably drew on real tensions: northern tribes never fully at home in a Judean dynasty, Hebron's loss of capital status, and the burdens of a growing royal state. The foreign guard (Kerethites, Pelethites, Gittites) fits what is known of royal guards in the region.
views.C: Critical scholars see Absalom's revolt as the center of the Succession Narrative. Some read it as an honest account by a court writer close to the events; others think it was shaped to defend Solomon's kingship. The chronology ("four" or "forty" years, 15:7) shows how the text was later copied and corrected.
views.L: The chapter is built around a procession: the king's household passing by at the edge of the city, the Kidron, the ascent of the Mount of Olives, the summit. At each stage someone meets David and must choose: Ittai, the priests, Hushai. Loyalty and betrayal are the theme, with Ahithophel as the hidden shadow.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition counted Ahithophel among those who have no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and drew from Absalom's "stealing hearts" the lesson that he stole three hearts (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). Psalm 3, "when he ran away from his son Absalom," is read as David's prayer in this flight.
views.X: Christian readers since the church fathers have seen in David's flight a foreshadowing of Jesus: the rejected king crossing the Kidron, weeping on the Mount of Olives, betrayed by a trusted friend (John 18:1; Luke 22:39; Psalm 41:9). Ittai's loyalty has been read as a model of discipleship.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three tests of loyalty at the city's edge
deep.b: This is my own reading. As David leaves Jerusalem, he gives three parties a chance to go back: Ittai the foreigner (15:19–20), the priests with the ark (15:25–27), and Hushai (15:33–34). Each is told to return, and each response shows a different kind of loyalty: Ittai refuses and follows David into danger; the priests obey and serve him by returning; Hushai obeys and serves him by pretending to betray him. David, who once used people as tools, now gives them a choice. I suggest the scene is designed to show a king who no longer "sends" (as in chapter 11) but releases. Commentators have noted David's changed manner here; the pattern of three releases is my own observation.

echoes: 1 Samuel 8:11; Ruth 1:16–17; Psalm 3:0; Psalm 41:9; Psalm 55:12–14; 1 Kings 1:5; Luke 19:37–41; Luke 22:39; John 18:1

settings.to: men from all the tribes of Israel who came to Jerusalem with lawsuits for the king
settings.when: after his return to favor, each morning by the road to the gate, until the time of his vow at Hebron (15:7)
settings.why: Absalom tells each man his case is good but the king has no one to hear it, and wishes he were judge. Then he kisses them instead of letting them bow. It is a campaign speech aimed at people who felt the king ignored them. The narrator says he "stole the hearts" of Israel. Readers see how a king who fails at justice opens the door to revolt.

settings.to: King David, in Jerusalem
settings.when: four years after the start of his campaign at the gate
settings.why: Absalom asks leave to pay a vow he says he made in Geshur: if the LORD brought him home, he would serve the LORD in Hebron. The religious excuse hides a revolt. David blesses him and sends him off. Readers know that Hebron was where David himself was first made king.

settings.to: all the tribes of Israel
settings.when: while he is at Hebron, claiming to pay a vow
settings.why: When the ram's horn sounds, they are to shout, "Absalom is king in Hebron!" Hebron was where David himself was first made king. The order shows the revolt was planned across the land, and that Absalom meant to repeat his father's rise.

settings.to: Ittai, leader of six hundred Philistine soldiers from Gath, and David
settings.when: as David flees Jerusalem
settings.why: David tells the foreigner, who just arrived, to go back and serve the new king. Ittai swears by the LORD that he will be with David "for death or for life." His words echo Ruth's to Naomi (Ruth 1:16–17). A Philistine shows more loyalty than David's own son. Readers see the kind of faithfulness David still inspires.

settings.to: Zadok the priest and the Levites carrying the ark
settings.when: at the Kidron Valley, as David leaves the city
settings.why: David will not take the ark with him as a weapon or a charm. If the LORD wants him, he will bring him back; if not, "let him do with me whatever looks good to him." Readers remember how Israel carried the ark into battle and lost it (1 Samuel 4:3–11). David's trust is in God himself.

settings.what: David's prayer and his plan with Hushai
settings.to: the LORD, and then his friend Hushai the Arkite
settings.when: on the Mount of Olives, after he learns Ahithophel has joined Absalom
settings.why: David prays, "LORD, please make Ahithophel's advice foolish." Moments later Hushai arrives, and David sends him back to pretend loyalty to Absalom and spoil Ahithophel's advice, with the priests' sons as messengers. Readers see prayer and planning side by side. God's answer to the prayer comes through Hushai (17:14).

title: Curses on the Road
sum: On the far side of the Mount of Olives, Ziba, the servant of Saul's grandson Mephibosheth, meets David with donkeys and food, and claims that his master hopes to win back Saul's kingdom. David gives Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property. At Bahurim, Shimei of Saul's clan curses David and throws stones, calling him a man of blood. Abishai wants to kill him, but David refuses: perhaps the LORD told him to curse, and perhaps the LORD will repay David with good.

In Jerusalem, Hushai greets Absalom with "Long live the king!" and offers his service, every word carefully two-sided. Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with the ten concubines David left behind, to make the break with his father final. A tent is pitched on the palace roof, and it happens in the sight of all Israel, as Nathan had said.
readings: Read as David under judgment

David accepts Shimei's curses as possibly sent by God, and the narrator shows Nathan's word coming true on the very roof where David's sin began. The chapter is the low point of David's life: deserted, cursed, his kingdom and his wives taken.
Read as a contest of words

Ziba's report, Shimei's curse, Hushai's greetings and Ahithophel's advice are all speeches whose truth the reader must weigh. Some are lies, some are half-truths, some are true in a way the speaker does not intend. The chapter trains the reader to listen carefully, as David must.

views.H: Shimei's accusation shows that many in Benjamin still blamed David for the fall of Saul's house. The custom of a new king taking the old king's women is attested across the ancient Near East.
views.C: Halpern and McKenzie argue that the books of Samuel were written partly to answer charges like Shimei's, that David was a usurper with blood on his hands. Many critical scholars read the Ziba and Mephibosheth scenes as part of a longer thread about Saul's house that continues in 19:16–30.
views.L: The chapter pairs two meetings outside the city (Ziba, Shimei) with two inside (Hushai, Ahithophel). Hushai's double meanings are among the finest examples of irony in the Bible. The roof of 16:22 links back to 11:2, closing a circle.
views.J: The rabbis praised David's restraint toward Shimei and read 16:10 as acceptance of divine judgment. They saw Ahithophel's advice as wickedly wise. The Talmud assumes he was Bathsheba's grandfather (Sanhedrin 69b) and gives his motive as ambition: he misread signs that kingship would come from his line (Sanhedrin 101b). The idea that he wanted revenge for Bathsheba comes from modern commentators.
views.X: Christian readers have compared David's silence under Shimei's curses with Jesus: "People heaped abuse on him, and he gave no abuse back" (1 Peter 2:23), and his "what do you and I have in common" with Jesus' words at Cana (John 2:4).

deep.b: David says Shimei may be cursing because "the LORD told him" (16:10–11). The Bible often speaks this way: God hardens Pharaoh's heart, sends an evil spirit on Saul, and later "incites" David to take a census (24:1). Readers have handled this in several ways. Traditional Jewish and Christian theology holds that God can use the free and sinful acts of people for his purposes without approving them, as Joseph says of his brothers (Genesis 50:20); Shimei is still held responsible (1 Kings 2:44). Some readers see David's words as humility, not doctrine: he refuses to defend himself because he knows he has sinned, even if not the sin Shimei names. Critical scholars note that ancient Israel tended to attribute all events to God and did not draw the lines later theology draws. David's "maybe" (16:12) keeps the question open: he hopes, but does not presume to know God's mind.

settings.to: David, then Ziba
settings.when: as David flees, just past the top of the Mount of Olives
settings.why: Ziba brings donkeys and food, and claims that Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get back Saul's kingdom. David at once gives Ziba everything that was Mephibosheth's. The quick grant, made on one man's word, sets up the hard case in 19:24–30, where Mephibosheth says Ziba lied.

settings.by: Shimei son of Gera, of Saul's clan
settings.to: King David and his men, as they pass Bahurim
settings.when: as David flees from Absalom
settings.why: Shimei calls David "a man stained with blood" and says the LORD is paying him back for the blood of Saul's house, whose throne he took. It is the charge the book has worked to answer. Readers hear what Saul's family and Benjamin said about David, and must weigh it against chapters 1–4 and 21.
views: Traditional readers think Shimei was wrong: David never killed any of Saul's family, and the deaths of Abner and Ish-bosheth were not his doing.
Scholars who read the book as royal apology think Shimei shows that many in Benjamin did blame David for these deaths, perhaps also for the execution of Saul's sons (21:1–9).

settings.to: Abishai and his other servants
settings.when: when Abishai offers to cut off Shimei's head
settings.why: David says the LORD may have told Shimei to curse him, and that if his own son wants him dead, a Benjaminite's curse is a small thing. Perhaps God will see his trouble and repay him with good. David accepts the curse as part of the judgment Nathan announced. Readers see the king humbled and trusting God.

settings.to: Absalom, in Jerusalem
settings.when: when Absalom asks why he did not leave with David
settings.why: Hushai says he belongs to the one "the LORD has chosen," and that he will serve the son as he served the father. Every word can be heard two ways. Absalom thinks it means him; readers know Hushai means David.

settings.to: Absalom and his followers
settings.when: when Absalom first takes Jerusalem
settings.why: Ahithophel tells Absalom to sleep with the ten concubines David left behind, in public, so there can be no going back and his supporters will grow bold. Absalom does it on the palace roof, where David first saw Bathsheba. Nathan's word in 12:11–12 is fulfilled to the letter.

title: Good Advice Undone
sum: Ahithophel proposes a quick strike: twelve thousand men, a pursuit that very night, panic in David's camp, and the death of David alone. Absalom and the elders like it, but Absalom asks Hushai's opinion. Hushai paints vivid pictures of David as a bear robbed of her cubs, hidden and dangerous, and proposes instead that Absalom gather all Israel and lead them himself. Absalom chooses Hushai's plan, "for the LORD had given orders to undo Ahithophel's good advice."

Hushai sends word through the priests and their sons, who escape Absalom's men by hiding in a well, protected by a quick-witted woman. David crosses the Jordan by morning. Ahithophel, seeing his advice ignored, goes home, sets his affairs in order and hangs himself. At Mahanaim, friends east of the Jordan bring David's tired army food and supplies.
readings: Read as providence through human choices

God does not appear in this chapter except in one sentence (17:14). Everything happens through human speech, spying, courage and choice. Yet the narrator says God was steering it all. Gerhard von Rad saw this hidden providence as the theology of the whole court story.
Read as a contest of counselors

Ahithophel's advice is brief, practical and right. Hushai's is long, flattering, full of pictures, and wrong for Absalom. The chapter shows how persuasion works on a vain leader: Hushai offers Absalom glory, and Absalom takes it.

views.H: David's escape across the Jordan to Mahanaim, a fortified town that had been Ish-bosheth's capital, was a sound military choice. The help of Shobi the Ammonite and Machir of Lo-debar shows David's network of alliances east of the Jordan.
views.C: Von Rad and later scholars see 17:14, with 11:27 and 12:24, as the theological keys to the Succession Narrative. Some critical scholars think these verses were added by an editor; others think the original author wrote history with this view of God built in.
views.L: The chapter is a masterpiece of suspense: the reader knows Hushai's plan, the messengers' danger, and the woman's trick, while Absalom's men do not. Ahithophel's quiet end, saddling his donkey and going home, contrasts with the noise of Hushai's speech.
views.J: The Mishnah lists Ahithophel among those who lose their share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). Rabbinic teaching took him as a warning that great wisdom without fear of God leads to ruin.
views.X: Christian readers have long paired Ahithophel with Judas: a trusted friend who betrayed his king and then hanged himself (Matthew 27:5; Psalm 41:9; John 13:18). The hiding of the messengers recalls Rahab, whom the New Testament praises (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the well and the roof
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The revolt chapters keep returning to high and low places. David's sin began on a roof (11:2), and Absalom's public act happens on the same roof (16:22). David's messengers are saved by going down into a well (17:18), and Absalom will end up in a pit in the forest (18:17). David goes up the Mount of Olives weeping (15:30) and up to the room over the gate weeping (18:33). I suggest the narrator uses height and depth as a moral map: those who climb to seize, fall; those who go down in humility are kept safe. Commentators have noted the roof link between 11:2 and 16:22; extending it into a pattern of high and low places is my own reading.

echoes: 15:31–37; 16:23; Joshua 2:1–7; 1 Samuel 19:11–17; Psalm 41:9; Psalm 55:12–14; Proverbs 19:21; Proverbs 21:30; Matthew 27:3–5; Acts 1:16–18

settings.to: Absalom and the elders of Israel
settings.when: the same day Absalom takes Jerusalem
settings.why: Ahithophel proposes to chase David that night with twelve thousand men while he is tired, kill only the king, and bring the people back to Absalom like a bride. The plan is sound, and all the elders agree. Readers know it would work, which makes what happens next the hand of God.

settings.to: Absalom and the men of Israel
settings.when: when Absalom asks him for a second opinion on Ahithophel's plan
settings.why: Hushai paints David and his men as angry bears and seasoned fighters, and warns that an early loss would make Israel panic. He flatters Absalom with a picture of himself leading a vast army, numberless as sand, to settle on David like dew. The speech buys David time to escape. The narrator explains that the LORD had decided to undo Ahithophel's good advice to bring ruin on Absalom (17:14). Readers see David's prayer in 15:31 answered.

title: O My Son Absalom
sum: David divides his army under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and stays behind at the troops' insistence, giving one public order: go easy on the young man Absalom. The battle is fought in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest kills more than the sword. Absalom, riding his mule, is caught by the head in a great oak and left hanging. A soldier refuses to touch him, remembering the king's order, but Joab drives three sticks into his heart and his armor bearers finish him. They throw him into a pit under a heap of stones.

Two runners carry the news. Ahimaaz arrives first but evades the question that matters. The Cushite arrives and answers it. David, shaken, climbs to the room over the gate and weeps: "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! Oh, if only I had died in your place."
readings: Read as victory and grief together

The battle saves David's kingdom, and the news that should be "good news" breaks his heart. The chapter refuses to separate the public and the private: the king wins, the father loses. Nathan's word that the sword would not leave David's house reaches its most painful point.
Read as justice and disobedience

Joab kills Absalom against the king's explicit order. Readers have judged him differently: as a loyal general who did what was necessary to end a civil war, or as a ruthless man who took into his own hands what belonged to the king. David never punishes him directly, but on his deathbed he remembers Joab's killings (1 Kings 2:5).

views.H: The battle east of the Jordan in rough, wooded country fits the geography of Gilead. A pillar called Absalom's Monument stood in the King's Valley in the writer's day; the tomb shown today in the Kidron Valley is from the first century AD.
views.C: Critical scholars regard the chapter as one of the finest pieces of Hebrew prose and a climax of the Succession Narrative. The contradiction between 14:27 (three sons) and 18:18 (no son) is often explained by different sources or by the death of the sons.
views.L: The chapter delays the news with two runners, a lookout and the king's repeated question, so that the reader feels David's dread. David's cry, five times "my son," is one of the most famous laments in literature, and inspired works from Renaissance motets to Faulkner's Absalom, Absalom!
views.J: The Mishnah draws measure-for-measure lessons: Absalom gloried in his hair and was hanged by it; he lay with ten concubines and ten men struck him; he stole three hearts and three sticks pierced him (Mishnah Sotah 1:8). The Talmud says David's eight cries of "my son" lifted Absalom out of Gehinnom into the world to come (Sotah 10b).
views.X: Many Christian readers set David's wish to die in his son's place beside the gospel, in which the Father gives his Son for rebels (Romans 5:8). Some contrast Absalom hanging on a tree for his own rebellion with Christ, who "became a curse" by hanging on a tree for others (Galatians 3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23).

deep.b: The soldier who saw Absalom hanging refused to kill him for a thousand pieces of silver, because the king had ordered him spared (18:12). Joab did not hesitate. Defenders of Joab argue that as long as Absalom lived, the war could break out again, and that David's love for his son had already cost the nation dearly (13:21; 14:24). On this view Joab saved the kingdom and David's life. Critics point out that Joab disobeyed a public command, killed a helpless man, and had a record of killing rivals on his own authority (Abner in 3:27; Amasa in 20:10). David does not punish Joab now, but the next chapter shows the strain between them (19:5–7, 13), and David's last instructions to Solomon include Joab's bloodshed (1 Kings 2:5–6). The text, as usual, reports and does not rule, but the honest soldier's speech (18:12–13) gives the reader a standard to measure Joab by.

deep.title: Claude's theory: between sky and ground
deep.b: This is my own reading. Absalom hangs "between the sky and the ground" (18:9), as if neither heaven nor earth will receive him. He wanted a monument to keep his name on the earth (18:18), but he is buried under a pile of stones in a forest pit (18:17). The same phrase is used of the angel with drawn sword over Jerusalem, "between the earth and the heavens," in the parallel to 2 Samuel 24 (1 Chronicles 21:16). I suggest the phrase marks a moment of judgment hanging in the balance, and that the narrator deliberately leaves Absalom suspended, so that the final word on his fate belongs to David's cry, not to Joab's darts. The rabbis' teaching that David's cries lifted Absalom from Gehinnom (Sotah 10b) points in the same direction; reading the phrase this way is my own suggestion.

echoes: Deuteronomy 21:18–23; Joshua 7:26; Joshua 8:29; 12:10; 14:25–27; 1 Kings 2:5–6; Isaiah 52:7; Exodus 32:32; Romans 9:3; Galatians 3:13

settings.to: his three commanders, Joab, Abishai and Ittai, in the hearing of the whole army
settings.when: at the gate of Mahanaim, as the army goes out to battle
settings.why: David asks them to go easy on "the young man, on Absalom," for his sake. The order puts the king's love for his son against the safety of the kingdom. Joab ignores it. Readers feel the torn father inside the king.

settings.what: "My son, my son": David's lament for Absalom
settings.to: no one but himself and his dead son, in the room above the gate of Mahanaim
settings.when: when the Cushite messenger tells him Absalom is dead
settings.why: David cries out that he wishes he had died instead of his son. It is grief, not a speech for anyone. Yet its effect on the army is serious, as Joab tells him the next morning. Many readers hear in it David's grief for his own sin, since Absalom's revolt was part of the judgment Nathan announced.
